# How to use this file

This lab is about **thinking**: you decide how to set up each analysis. The file reads the data and draws plots for you; **you** identify the variables, decide the scale types and factor types, and write the model. Do not fit any model yet: that is Lab 9b. Fill every `Your answer` line; this becomes step 1 of your write-up.

* The data are the **raw files** from the course website: `wworm1.txt`, `wworm2.txt` and `LeprosyScores.txt`.
  The raw files are laid out as in the handout (one row per line of the field or per patient, treatments side by side),
  so a short helper reshapes them into **one row per observation**, which is the format `lm()` needs.
* Base R only. Run chunk by chunk or **Knit**.
* Work in groups to decide how to analyse each data set.

## Reading the raw data

```{r data-helpers}
# Where the raw data files live on the course website
data_url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DavidCSchneider/StatisticalScience/refs/heads/main/Data/Labs/"

# Read the first `nrows` lines of a raw text file (the files end with free-text notes that we skip).
# If the file is in your working folder it is used; otherwise it is downloaded from the website.
read_raw <- function(file, nrows) {
  src <- if (file.exists(file)) file else paste0(data_url, file)
  read.table(src, nrows = nrows)
}

# Latin square files: 5 lines (= rows of the field) x 10 numbers = 5 pairs (T, N), one pair per column of the field.
# as.vector() reads a matrix column by column, so row varies fastest, as in the Minitab "stack" commands.
latin_long <- function(raw) {
  m <- as.matrix(raw)
  data.frame(plot   = 1:25,
             trtmnt = as.vector(m[, seq(1, 9, by = 2)]),   # T: treatment code (0 = control, 1-4 = fumigants)
             count  = as.vector(m[, seq(2, 10, by = 2)]),  # N: wireworms per plot
             col    = rep(1:5, each = 5),
             row    = rep(1:5, times = 5))
}

# Leprosy file: 10 patients (lines) x 6 numbers = (before, after) for TRI, TRII and Control side by side.
leprosy_long <- function(raw) {
  m <- as.matrix(raw)
  data.frame(patient   = 1:30,                    # 30 different patients
             treatment = rep(c("TRI", "TRII", "Control"), each = 10),
             before    = c(m[, 1], m[, 3], m[, 5]),
             after     = c(m[, 2], m[, 4], m[, 6]))
}
```

## The recipe (Lab 9b write-up, handout)

| Step | What to do |
|:--|:--|
| 1 | **Construct the model**: list response and explanatory variables; assign symbols, units and scale type; write the statistical model (Lab 9a). |
| 2 | **Execute the model** and plot the residuals against the fitted values. |
| 3 | **Evaluate assumptions**: residuals homogeneous (residual vs fit plot)? normal (histogram, quantile or normal score plot)? If not met, a randomization p-value may be necessary. |
| 4 | **ANOVA**: Report origin of variation, df, sum of squares (the amount of variation attributed to each source); calculate the likelihood ratio (LR) for the full model (Quick check of whether the model explains enough to be worth testing term by term). If the evidence is negligible (LR < 20) report LR and the table; otherwise go on to step 7. |
| 7 | **ANOVA**: calculate MS, F and the Type I error (p-values); report the full table. |
| 9 | **Decisions**: first any **interaction** terms (p < alpha: reject H0; p >= alpha: cannot reject). If significant, interpret. If interactions are not significant, decide about the fixed factors and regression terms, then report slopes or means for the significant terms. |

**The three data sets.** All three are **counts**. Counts often have heterogeneous errors (the variance grows with the mean), so you must look at how severe the heterogeneity is, what to do about it, and whether a recomputed p-value by randomization is needed.

Data source: Snedecor and Cochran (1980) *Statistical Methods*, 7th ed., Iowa State University Press.

\newpage

# Part 1 (Lab 9a): Setting up the analysis

Setting up is the most important and most difficult part of the analysis: it needs unfamiliar abstract thinking (identify variables, invent names for variables that include several categories, decide the measurement scale, separate response from explanatory variables). Questions to ask about **every** data set:

1. What was **measured** on each unit (response)? What are the **units** (plots, patients, ...)?

2. What was **manipulated** or recorded as a possible explanation (explanatory variables)?

3. For each variable: **nominal** (categories), **ordinal**, **interval** or **ratio**? Sometimes numeric *codes* can be labels.

4. Is each factor **fixed** (levels chosen on purpose; inference only to these levels) or **random** (levels sampled from a population)?

5. Are factors **crossed** or **nested**? Can interactions be estimated (is there replication)?

6. Could a numeric variable be a **covariate** (regression term) rather than a factor?

## Data set 1: wireworms in a Latin square (wworm1)

Snedecor and Cochran (1980) p. 289. **N** = number of wireworms per 9 x 9 x 5 inch plot; **T** = treatment: control (0) and 4 soil fumigants (1-4).
Plots are arranged in a 5 x 5 array.

**Take a look at the data first** before exploring

```{r d1-import}
w1_raw <- read_raw("wworm1.txt", nrows = 5)   # raw file: 5 lines x 10 numbers
w1_raw                                           # look at the raw layout first
w1 <- latin_long(w1_raw)                         # reshape: one row per plot
w1
str(w1)                           # check how R read each column
```

The layout of the field: treatment code (left) and count (right) in each row x column.

```{r d1-layout}
with(w1, tapply(trtmnt, list(row = row, col = col), identity))   # treatment in each plot
with(w1, tapply(count,  list(row = row, col = col), identity))   # count in each plot
```

```{r d1-explore, fig.width=7, fig.height=3.6, fig.cap="Wireworm counts by treatment, row and column."}
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
stripchart(count ~ trtmnt, data = w1, vertical = TRUE, method = "jitter", pch = 16,
           xlab = "Treatment (0 = control)", ylab = "Wireworms per plot")
boxplot(count ~ row, data = w1, xlab = "Row", ylab = "Wireworms per plot")
boxplot(count ~ col, data = w1, xlab = "Column", ylab = "Wireworms per plot")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

```{r d1-spread, fig.height=3.4, fig.cap="Variance against mean for each treatment (data set 1)."}
m1 <- tapply(w1$count, w1$trtmnt, mean)       # mean count per treatment
v1 <- tapply(w1$count, w1$trtmnt, var)        # variance per treatment
round(rbind(mean = m1, variance = v1, variance_over_mean = v1 / m1), 2)
plot(m1, v1, pch = 16, xlab = "Treatment mean", ylab = "Treatment variance")
```

4. Write the model in GLM format. Can any interaction term be estimated? Why or why not?

> **Your answer:** \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_
>
> \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

Treatment ($T$) is Fixed because the 5 specific treatment levels (Control and 4 soil fumigants) were deliberately chosen on purpose by the experimenter

Row ($R$) and Column ($C$) are Random because they act as factors representing spatial location variations within the $5 \times 5$ field grid. The researcher does not care about testing Row 1 versus Row 4 as specific treatments of interest.

5. Count variation relative to both random factors, Pct variance = (SS$_{rows}$ + SS$_{cols}$) / SS$_{total}$. Calculate it (model with rows and columns only).

```{r d1-pct}
# Hint: fit count against the factors row and col only (no treatment), look at the SS column of anova(),
# then use the sums of squares in the formula above.
a1 <- anova(lm(count ~ factor(row) + factor(col), data = w1))
a1
SS_rows = a1["factor(row)", "Sum Sq"]
SS_rows
SS_cols = a1["factor(col)", "Sum Sq"]
SS_cols
SS_total = sum(a1[, "Sum Sq"])
100*(SS_rows + SS_cols)/SS_total
(a1["factor(row)", "Sum Sq"] + a1["factor(col)", "Sum Sq"]) / sum(a1[, "Sum Sq"]) * 100   # per cent
```

> **Your answer:** \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

3 sources of variation: (1) Random error (2) Treatment (3) location of the plot (soil)

This tells us how much of the variation in wireworm counts is attributable to where the plot sits in the field, rather than to the treatment or random error? They were built into the design because the researchers expected the field to vary, for example in soil, moisture or wireworm density. 

About 34% of the variation in counts is associated with a plot’s row and column position. Including rows and columns in the model removes this variation from the error term, giving a more precise test of the treatment effect.

## Data set 2: the wireworm experiment repeated one year later (wworm2)

Snedecor and Cochran (1980) p. 273. The same experiment (same 5 treatments, 5 x 5 Latin square) **repeated one year later**.
This design does not have a name, so you cannot look it up: use what you have learned to set it up.

**Take a look at the data first** before exploring

```{r d2-import}
w2 <- latin_long(read_raw("wworm2.txt", nrows = 5))   # same layout as wworm1.txt
str(w2)
with(w2, tapply(trtmnt, list(row = row, col = col), identity))   # layout in year 2
# Treatment layout
with(w2, tapply(count,  list(row = row, col = col), identity))   # counts in year 2
# Count layout
```

```{r d2-both, fig.width=7, fig.height=3.8, fig.cap="Wireworm counts by treatment in the two years."}
both <- rbind(data.frame(w1, year = "1"), data.frame(w2, year = "2"))   # the two experiments in one data frame
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
stripchart(count ~ trtmnt, data = both[both$year == "1", ], vertical = TRUE, method = "jitter", pch = 16,
           ylim = range(both$count), main = "Year 1", xlab = "Treatment", ylab = "Wireworms per plot")
stripchart(count ~ trtmnt, data = both[both$year == "2", ], vertical = TRUE, method = "jitter", pch = 16,
           ylim = range(both$count), main = "Year 2", xlab = "Treatment", ylab = "Wireworms per plot")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
round(tapply(both$count, list(year = both$year, trt = both$trtmnt), mean), 1)   # means by year and treatment
round(tapply(both$count, both$year, var), 1)                                     # variance in each year
```

## Data set 3: leprosy bacilli before and after treatment (leprosy)

Snedecor and Cochran (1980) p. 368. Scores of leprosy bacilli **before (B)** and **after (A)** treatment with two antibiotics (TRI, TRII)
and one control, 10 patients per treatment.

**Take a look at the data first** before exploring


```{r d3-import}
lp_raw <- read_raw("LeprosyScores.txt", nrows = 10)   # raw file: 10 lines x 6 numbers
lp_raw                                                  # columns: before/after for TRI, TRII, Control
lp <- leprosy_long(lp_raw)                              # one row per patient
str(lp)
head(lp, 10)
```

```{r d3-explore, fig.width=7, fig.height=3.8, fig.cap="Leprosy: after against before (left) and scores by treatment (right)."}
lp$treatment <- factor(lp$treatment, levels = c("Control", "TRI", "TRII"))   # label order: control first
cols <- c(Control = "black", TRI = "red", TRII = "blue")
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(lp$before, lp$after, pch = 16, col = cols[as.character(lp$treatment)],
     xlab = "Score before treatment", ylab = "Score after treatment")
abline(0, 1, lty = 2)                                   # no change line
legend("topleft", legend = names(cols), col = cols, pch = 16, bty = "n")
boxplot(after ~ treatment, data = lp, xlab = "Treatment", ylab = "Score after treatment")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
round(rbind(mean_before = tapply(lp$before, lp$treatment, mean),
            mean_after  = tapply(lp$after,  lp$treatment, mean),
            sd_after    = tapply(lp$after,  lp$treatment, sd)), 2)
```

3. List **at least three different models** that could answer the question, with the response variable and explanatory variables of each.
   For each, write the model in GLM format and say what assumption it makes about the before score.

| Model | Response | Explanatory | GLM format | Assumption about the before score |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| M1 | A | Trt | $A = \beta_0 + Trt + \epsilon$ | Ignored |
| M2 | change = A - B | Trt | $(A-B) = \beta_0 + Trt + \epsilon$ (one-way ANOVA) | Effect of B on A is exactly 1:1 (slope fixed at 1) |
| M3 | A | B (covariate) + Trt | $A = \beta_0 + \beta B + Trt + \epsilon$ (**ANCOVA**) | Slope estimated from the data; assumes the same slope in all groups |
